name: Montana
summary_text: A trans visitor to Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records. A visitor's documents may therefore mismatch presentation at the border or at checkpoints. Screening carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country. Montana's own legal position is unusually favourable relative to its statute book. The state has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states for trans people, but Montana's courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined those laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions that were enacted have consequently not taken full effect, and that court record improved Montana's standing in the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment. Montana was the only state to improve in the 2026 rankings. The protections are judicial rather than statutory, so they depend on continued litigation. Nationally the youth-side picture remains unstable as federal policy shifts and litigation proceed. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court. Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

sources.title: Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. (June 15, 2020) - U.S. Supreme Court
sources.documents: Establishes federal Title VII protection against workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity as sex discrimination, applicable in Montana despite lack of state statute.
sources.detail: Consolidated with Altitude Express v. Zarda and R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC; cited by Montana courts in SB 99 case. Complements Montana Executive Orders: 2000 Gov. Marc Racicot personnel rules, Nov 2008 Gov. Brian Schweitzer EO 41-2008, Jan 2016 Gov. Steve Bullock expansion to gender identity and contractors. No URL visible.

sources.title: Censure and barring of Rep. Zooey Zephyr (April 2023) - documented enforcement incident
sources.documents: Incident showing state-house enforcement against openly trans lawmaker after opposition to SB 99; protest policing, 7 arrests, exclusion from floor until adjournment.
sources.detail: April 18, 2023 remarks on SB 99 ('tantamount to torture,' 'blood on your hands'); Montana Freedom Caucus misgendering statement; Speaker Matt Regier denied speaking; April 24 rally ~100 people, gallery chant 'let her speak,' riot police clearance, 7 arrested and released without bail; April 26 House vote 68-32 along party lines to bar from floor, gallery, antechamber. No URL visible.

name: Nebraska
summary_text: Nebraska is a state within the United States, and the national framework sets the first layer of exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and the ACLU is litigating the policy on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with separate guidance available from Lambda Legal on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.  State policy reinforces the federal line. Executive Order 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023 and titled a Women's Bill of Rights, defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, and commits the state to sex-based segregation in athletics, bathrooms and changing rooms on the stated basis of biological differences in athletic ability and safety. A visitor dealing with Nebraska state agencies, state buildings or state-run sporting venues should expect to be classified by sex assigned at birth.  Entry and screening follow national rather than state procedure. In February 2025 the State Department announced it would refuse visas to transgender athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flagging applicants with an internal marking and treating a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. TSA screening at airports can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that carry an outing risk for visitors whose presentation does not match their documents.  Custody is a documented site of harm in Nebraska. Federal courts held in August 2022 that Nebraska prison officials were not liable for their treatment of a transgender inmate identified as Jane Doe, who was housed by sex assigned at birth in a men's prison, diagnosed with gender dysphoria and placed in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who assaulted her. District Judge Brian C. Buescher dismissed her failure-to-treat, denial-of-surgery and failure-to-protect claims, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could find deliberate indifference to her medical need and that she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. National prison policy is aligned with that placement: the Federal Bureau of Prisons rescinded its 2017 guidance permitting transfer to facilities matching gender identity in May 2018, and from 2026 has adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style measures for transgender inmates, including hair cutting, hormone withdrawal and substitution of psychiatric medication, while ceasing to report how many transgender prisoners it holds.

sources.title: Bostock v. Clayton County, U.S. Supreme Court
sources.documents: Holds workplace discrimination on basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination under Title VII; basis for employment protections in Nebraska
sources.detail: Decided June 15, 2020, consolidated with Altitude Express, Inc. v. Zarda and R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes Inc. v. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
